newsitem.title: SPAIN: INTERVIEW-Euro to provide chances for Spain banks.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Euro to provide chances for Spain banks.

text.p: Spanish banks can look forward to fresh business opportunities from the launch of Europe's common currency in markets both at home and abroad, said Juan Bengoechea, director of Banco Bilbao Vizcaya's euro team.

The world's top half dozen global financial institutions will slug it out in London, Paris and Frankfurt for the business of multinational companies, but canny Spanish banks have room to gain market share, Bengoechea told Reuters in an interview.

"Spain can play a secondary role," Bengoechea said on Wednesday. "The struggle for Spain is to recognise its limits and to try to fight for certain areas, like the secondary share market, which is more tied to local companies," he said.

In particular, Bengoechea, who has been preparing Spain's largest banking group for the euro for the past year, pointed to domestic opportunities in the share market, in fund management, and in services to small and medium-sized companies as well as in its function as a gateway to Europe for Latin America.

For Spanish banks, adapting to the euro is particularly thorny. Not only will the expected 1999 launch do away with the peseta, but preparations for the euro have already permanently altered the entire banking environment.

Once a country with a weak currency and high inflation, Spain has become, within little more than a year, a country with a stable currency, low inflation and, as a result -- historically low short- and long-term interest rates.
Investors once content with a safe, full-yielding fixed-income interest product are on the prowl for richer gains -- and the bourse is surging from record to record.
"The share markets are much more attractive so we will reinforce our (investment) funds. There will be tough competition...and investors will switch to the best-managed," Bengoechea said.
In addition, Bengoechea said there was market share to be won preparing small- and medium-sized companies, the backbone of the Spanish economy, for the single currency launch.

"An overwhelming majority of clients expect banks to resolve their problems. Some 80 percent or more of small-and medium-companies haven't done any preparations and they expect banks to solve the problems," he said.

Most spectaculary, BBV -- and its key domestic rival Santander -- have responded to the approach of the euro by expanding aggressively in Latin America where high growth rates will help cushion declining margins at home.
"The topic of the euro is tightly tied to the topic of Latin America which is a process of geographic diversification.
"The fight is in what measure Latin America will diversify into currencies other than the dollar. We want to bet strongly on being the bank of the euro in Latin America," he said.
BBV earnings were boosted in the first quarter by earnings in Latin America, where it continues to show a hearty appetite for new buys with purchases in Mexico, Colombia and Argentina.

Exluding Latin American holdings, the bank's ordinary margin, which reflects loan, commission and own-account trading earnings, would only have risen 11 percent instead of the 33.8 percent jump it registered overall in the first quarter.
But much depends on the sophistication of the bank's internal systems.
"Risk control is going to play a key role. One has to have perfectly adjusted accounting systems that match risk to yields so one knows where one is losing and where one is earning money," he said.
Bengoechea said the bank would conduct trial runs on its computing systems in the second half of 1998 and would be ready to go on January 1, 1999 in the euro as well as the peseta.
Training programs for personnel have been stepped up.
"Whoever is better prepared than the competition for the transition will win market share," Bengoechea said.
